newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU reacts positively to greater BoE independence.
newsitem.headline: EU reacts positively to greater BoE independence.

text.p: European Union officials reacted positively on Tuesday to Britain's plan to give the Bank of England greater independence in setting monetary policy, a step towards meeting the criteria for a single currency.

Although many still believe it is unlikely that Britain will join a single currency in 1999, the new Labour government's more constructive approach towards Europe has been greeted with both relief and optimism.
"It's a good step in the right direction," said a senior EU monetary official.
Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, on Tuesday announced substantial steps towards independence for the Bank of England, but stopped short of giving it full autonomy.
The decision was widely seen as an effort towards fulfilling one of the criteria for economic and monetary union -- central bank independence.

Yet given that Britain remains outside Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism -- another Maastricht treaty requirement -- there is little hope that it could qualify for the euro ahead of the 1999 launch date.
Brown told a news conference it was unlikely that Britain would be an EMU member in 1999.

Public hostility towards the single currency, the Labour government's promise of a referendum on the issue, and the recent instability of sterling, were also cited by officials as factors arguing against early euro membership.
A more likely scenario would be for Britain to join the euro bloc before the introduction of banknotes and coins in 2002.
Under Brown's plan the British central bank now has "operational responsiblity" for setting interest rates to meet an inflation target laid down by the Treasury.
The fact that the Treasury still retains the right to set an inflation target is what prevents Britain from meeting the independent central bank test.

Britain negotiated an opt-out to the single currency during the Maastricht treaty's negotiations. Under the agreement the new Labour government would have to decide by the end of this year whether it wanted to be considered for EMU membership in 1999.
Failure to do so would more than likely eliminate Britain's chance for early membership, officials said.
